# 佛說盂蘭盆經

**ID:** T0685
**Volume:** T16
**Category:** 經集部類
**Original Category:** 經集部
**Byline:** 西晉 竺法護譯
**Dynasty:** 西晉
**Date:** 266–313
**Juans:** 1
**CBETA:** https://cbetaonline.dila.edu.tw/zh/T0685

## Contributors
- 竺法護 (A000749)

## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

T685 in one fascicle is the famous *Yúlánpén jīng* — the scriptural foundation of the Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese Buddhist Ghost Festival (中元節 / 盂蘭盆會, Jp. *Obon*), celebrated annually on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month. The Taishō colophon attributes the translation to [Dharmarakṣa](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) of the Western Jìn (西晉月氏三藏竺法護譯). The sūtra recounts how the disciple Maudgalyāyana (大目乾連 / Mùlián), having attained the six superknowledges, sees his deceased mother reborn as a hungry ghost and learns from the Buddha that her release requires the collective offerings of the *saṅgha* on the day of *pravāraṇā* (僧自恣日), the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

**Abstract**

Although the text-internal date and the [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) attribution are conventional, modern scholarship — most influentially Iwamoto Yutaka 岩本裕 (1968) — has argued that the *Yúlánpén jīng* is not in fact a translation from Sanskrit / Indic but a Chinese-composed apocryphon (*疑偽經*) created sometime between the late Eastern Hàn and the early Liùcháo, drawing on Chinese ritual and ancestor-cult sensibilities and grafting them onto the Indic Mūlasarvāstivādin Maudgalyāyana legends. The non-Indic etymology of *yúlánpén* 盂蘭盆 (variously hypothesized as *avalambana* "hanging upside down," but with severe phonological problems) and the sūtra's celebration of post-mortem filial obligation in distinctly Chinese terms support this view. Nonetheless, the sūtra's enormous ritual and cultural footprint in East-Asian Buddhism is matched by few other texts. The conventional [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) attribution gives a working bracket of 265 (the founding of the Western Jìn) to 311 (the Yǒngjiā disorders), but the actual date of composition is uncertain and may post-date [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) (b. c. 230 – d. c. 308).

The text was the object of intensive medieval commentary — see *[Zōngmì's Yúlánpén jīng shū 盂蘭盆經疏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0365)* (T1792), the most influential Tang commentary, and the cluster of Sòng commentaries from [KR6i0367](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0367) ([元照](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%85%83%E7%85%A7) *Xīnjì* 新記) through [KR6i0368](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0368) ([普觀](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%AE%E8%A7%80) *Huìgǔ tōngjīn jì*), [KR6i0370](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0370) ([遇榮](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%81%87%E6%A6%AE) *Xiàohéng chāo* 孝衡鈔), and [KR6i0371](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0371) ([日新](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%97%A5%E6%96%B0) *Yúyì* 餘義). A Míng "new commentary" by [智旭](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%BA%E6%97%AD) is preserved as [KR6i0372](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0372), and a Qīng commentary by [靈耀](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%9D%88%E8%80%80) as [KR6i0373](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0373). The sūtra is closely related to a shorter Chinese variant, [KR6i0376](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0376) (T686 *Bàoēn fèngpén jīng* 報恩奉盆經, attributed to "失譯" / unknown translator) — which the *Taishō* itself notes as a parallel to T685 — and to the wider cluster of Maudgalyāyana–Mother narratives.
